title: Microsoft Steps In to Kill LG Monitor Adware After User Backlash
excerpt: Windows boss Pavan Davuluri pressured LG into disabling McAfee pop-up ads that the company's monitors were silently installing on PCs, but the underlying mechanism remains intact.
body:
• LG monitors were silently installing an app via Windows Update that served McAfee pop-up ads on users' desktops — including on the company's $1,200 UltraGear gaming display.
  • Microsoft's Windows chief Pavan Davuluri intervened after Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney flagged the issue, getting LG to agree to disable the McAfee pop-up.
  • The underlying Windows mechanism that allows hardware makers to silently install software remains unchanged, leaving the door open for future abuse.
  • LG defended the practice, claiming McAfee was never installed without consent — a characterisation critics and users have challenged.

Microsoft has pressured LG Electronics into disabling McAfee antivirus pop-up ads that the Korean electronics giant's monitors were quietly pushing onto Windows PCs. The intervention came after weeks of user complaints and a pointed public callout from Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney.

Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft's executive vice president for Windows and devices, confirmed the move on X on July 22. "We've connected with the team at LG and as an immediate next step, they have agreed to disable the McAfee pop-up from their app," he wrote, adding that Microsoft would "keep improving here with our ecosystem partners."

How the Adware Got There

The controversy traces back several weeks, when LG monitor owners began reporting a mysterious "LG Monitor App Installer" appearing on their PCs without their knowledge or consent. The app, it turned out, was being distributed through Windows Update alongside routine display drivers.

https://x.com/Pirat_Nation/status/2080307196047372682

YouTube channel Gamers Nexus published an investigation documenting the process after receiving a flood of user reports. Their testing showed that simply connecting an LG UltraGear 34GX900A-B — a gaming monitor with a retail price close to $1,200 — to a Windows PC triggered the silent installation. At no point was the user informed, according to Gamers Nexus.

Once installed, the app served pop-up ads for McAfee's "free 30-day trial" on every boot, according to the investigation. It also promoted LG's own streaming service, LG Channels. The app was automatically granted access to "all system resources" and the user's internet connection, Gamers Nexus reported.

The problem wasn't limited to new hardware. Gamers Nexus found the app was also installing itself on older LG monitors, widening the scope of affected users considerably.

The Backlash Builds

The issue gained momentum on Reddit, where multiple users documented the uninvited software. It hit critical mass when Tom Warren of The Verge took to X on July 23 to vent his own frustrations — not just with LG monitors, but with the company's smart TVs as well.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=zZjMd-kttxQ

"Honestly, fuck LG for adding these notifications at startup on their TVs. I had every option for promotions disabled in the system settings, but they added new ones through the built in apps."

— Tom Warren, The Verge

But it was Tim Sweeney's post tagging Davuluri that forced a response from Microsoft. Within hours, the Windows boss confirmed LG had agreed to pull the McAfee advertising from the app. References to McAfee were subsequently removed from the LG Monitor App Installer listing in the Microsoft Store, according to The Register.

LG's Defence Falls Flat

LG responded to the furore with a statement to TechRadar that critics found unconvincing. "LG Electronics reiterates that McAfee is not installed automatically and is never installed without the user's explicit consent," the company said, adding that the installer was "distributed through Microsoft's official Windows distribution process, which included McAfee as an option."

The statement drew a distinction between the McAfee pop-up ad and actually installing the antivirus software — a technicality that missed the point for most users. As Gizmodo noted, "It's the kind of backwards thinking that misses the reason why customers were so annoyed in the first place."

LG also addressed separate privacy concerns raised by Gamers Nexus, which discovered that the app's consent terms referenced wiretapping and eavesdropping laws. The company said its TVs "do not collect, record, or store ambient conversations" and that voice recognition is an "optional, user-initiated feature."

The Bigger Problem Remains

While the McAfee ads are gone, the mechanism that enabled them is not. Windows includes a documented process that allows hardware manufacturers to silently install software when a device is first connected. As The Register noted, LG wasn't exploiting a vulnerability — it was using a legitimate, Microsoft-sanctioned pathway.

That pathway has no meaningful guardrails against abuse. The only consequence for companies that push unwanted software through this channel is the possibility of a bad app rating in the Microsoft Store.

LG isn't the only offender. Users have reported similar silent installations from Samsung and Razer peripherals, with Razer's Synapse software automatically downloading when any of the company's devices — from mice to webcams — are plugged in. Razer then prompts users to install additional apps like Razer Cortex.

What This Means for Consumers

For the millions of Indian consumers and tech professionals in the diaspora who rely on LG monitors — the brand is one of the most popular display makers in India and globally — the episode is a reminder that even premium hardware can come with hidden software costs. LG's UltraGear line is widely used by gamers and professionals across Indian tech communities in the US, and the silent adware installation caught many off guard.

Microsoft's intervention is a start, but it's a patch on a systemic issue. Until Windows tightens its review procedures for auto-installed device software, any hardware maker can use the same pipeline to push ads, bloatware, or worse onto users' machines. Davuluri's promise to "keep improving" has yet to translate into policy changes.
